rejected.title: Leaders of the new nation
card: George Washington
Led the Continental Army, then presided over the Constitutional Convention in 1787. He became the first president in 1789 and set early examples for the office.
James Madison
A Virginian who did much to plan the Constitution. He wanted a strong national government with powers split between its branches.
Alexander Hamilton
Washington's first Treasury secretary. He backed strong national power and wanted the national government to take on the states' war debts.
Patrick Henry
A Virginian who opposed the Constitution. He feared a strong national government would threaten the liberty of the states and their people.
rejected.remember: The new nation's leaders agreed on needing a government, but argued over how much power it should hold.

a.q: Which leader opposed the Constitution because he feared a strong national government?
a.why: Patrick Henry feared that a strong national government would threaten liberty. Madison, Hamilton and Washington all backed a stronger national government, so choosing one of them means mixing up their roles.
a.clue: Which leader on the card argued against the new plan?

b.q: A student says the new nation's leaders all wanted the same government. Which fact from the card shows this is wrong?
opts: Henry feared national power, while Hamilton backed it
Washington led the army, Madison planned the Constitution
Henry and Madison both came from the state of Virginia
Washington became president, while Hamilton ran the Treasury
b.why: Henry feared a strong national government, while Hamilton wanted strong national power. That is a real disagreement over power. The other options are true, but they describe jobs or home states, which do not show leaders disagreeing.
b.clue: Look for a difference in views on power, not in jobs.

b.q: Two leaders disagreed about the Constitution. Which pair held opposing views on how much power the national government should have?
b.why: Henry feared a strong national government, while Madison wanted one with powers split between branches. Madison, Hamilton and Washington all backed a stronger national government, so any pair made only of them does not show a disagreement over power. Henry and Madison both came from Virginia, but that does not mean they agreed.
b.clue: Only one leader on the card opposed the Constitution.

problems.detail: The clue 'Only one leader on the card opposed the Constitution' points straight to Henry, and only one option includes Henry. Combined with question a, a student can pick the answer without understanding the disagreement over power.

'Held opposing views on how much power the national government should have' is not tied to the ratification debate. Madison and Hamilton famously split in the 1790s over the national bank and how broadly to read federal power. A well-read Year 12 student could defend 'Madison and Hamilton'. The stem should say 'during the debate over ratifying the Constitution' or similar.
